paras: The killing of a railroad survey superintendent near Spring Hill, Louisiana, took place in early January 1903, after whitecaps had repeatedly ordered his surveying corps to discharge its Black cooks or leave the parish. The superintendent, who was not named, was found dead, killed by what the report called "party or parties unknown." The only account found is a short Marshall, Texas, dispatch in the Houston Daily Post that relayed a letter from a member of the crew.

The surveying corps was at work on the line of the Louisiana and Arkansas railroad, and one of its members, Charley Raguet, wrote from Spring Hill to W. Y. Allen of Marshall, Texas. According to the letter, the citizens of the parish the crew was passing through possessed "an antipathy for negroes." Whitecaps had repeatedly served notice on the corps to discharge its "negro cooks" or leave the parish.

The crew disregarded the threats. On a Monday morning, apparently January 5, the superintendent went alone ahead of the party to map out some work. When the others caught up with him, they found him dead. The letter did not name the killers or say how many there were, and it did not state that the whitecaps were responsible, though it placed the killing directly after their threats.
No report of an inquest, arrest, or trial appears in the coverage, and the parish where the killing occurred is not named.

The Houston Daily Post carried the story on January 10, 1903, under the headline "Assassinated in Louisiana," as a dispatch from Marshall dated the day before. The item repeated the letter's account without comment and gave neither the victim's name nor his race. No other white paper and no Black newspaper was found to have reported the killing.

accounts.label: Survey crew member's letter (via Marshall dispatch)
accounts.gist: Whitecaps in a parish hostile to Black people repeatedly ordered the corps to discharge its Black cooks or leave; the threats were ignored, and the superintendent was later found dead, killed by unknown persons.

framing.detail: Short dispatch headed 'Assassinated in Louisiana' relays the letter without comment, placing the whitecap threats and the killing side by side without stating a link.
